title: Processes, signals, jobs
subtitle: See what is running, stop it politely, and understand what systemd already knows.
objectives: List and filter processes by user, name, and resource use
Interpret process states, parents, and load averages
Send the right signal with kill and pkill
Move work between foreground and background
Use systemd tools to see a service as a group of processes

sections.title: A process is a running program

commands.desc: List every process with full command lines.
Find processes by name with arguments.
Show memory and swap in human units.
Sample system activity once per second, five times.
Politely ask a process to terminate.
Signal processes by owner and name.
List background jobs in the current shell.
Show resource use by systemd cgroup.

lab.title: Practice polite termination
lab.scenario: Create a controlled process, inspect it, move it around, and stop it without resorting to SIGKILL.

steps.text: Start a long sleep in the background.
steps.verify: The shell prints a job number and PID.

steps.text: List jobs and locate the process independently.
steps.verify: jobs shows the sleep job, and pgrep -a sleep shows the same PID and command.

steps.text: Inspect the process parent and state.
steps.verify: ps should show the sleep process, its parent PID, and a sleeping state.

steps.text: Send SIGTERM and confirm it exits.
steps.verify: After SIGTERM, the sleep process should disappear and jobs should no longer list it.

steps.text: Check memory and load for context.
steps.verify: free -h should report memory and swap, and uptime should report the load averages.

quiz.q: Which signal should you try first to stop a service process?
quiz.why: SIGTERM asks the process to terminate cleanly. SIGKILL cannot be caught and skips cleanup.

quiz.q: What does Ctrl+Z do to a foreground process?
quiz.why: Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP, suspending the job. Use bg to resume in the background or fg to return.

quiz.q: What does a high load average with low CPU usage often indicate?
options: Processes blocked on I/O in D state
quiz.why: Linux load includes uninterruptible tasks. Storage stalls can push load up while CPU sits idle.
